question: Should a PE-backed company hire a fractional CRO?
body:
## Direct Answer
For most PE-backed companies, a fractional CRO is a strong fit during the first 6 to 18 months of a hold, when you need senior revenue leadership to diagnose the go-to-market engine, fix pipeline math, and de-risk the number without committing $400K-plus in base salary to a full-time hire. It is the right call when the revenue problem is diagnostic and structural rather than a matter of adding headcount, and when the board wants operating rigor faster than a traditional executive search can deliver. It is the wrong call when the company needs a durable, culture-defining leader to recruit and hold a large quota-carrying team through a multi-year scale-up.

Private equity ownership changes the physics of the revenue org: the clock is shorter, the reporting is heavier, and every quarter is measured against a model that was underwritten before you arrived. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer — a seasoned operator who runs your commercial function two to three days a week on a contract — has become one of the most common first moves a sponsor makes inside a newly acquired company. But "common" is not the same as "correct for you." This essay walks through when the math works, when it does not, how to structure the engagement so it actually moves the number, and how to avoid the failure modes that turn a fractional CRO into an expensive consultant who leaves no residue.

## What problem is a PE-backed company actually trying to solve when it considers a fractional CRO?

The honest answer is rarely "we need someone to sell." It is almost always one of three underlying problems, and naming the right one determines whether fractional is the correct structure. The first is a **diagnosis problem**: the sponsor underwrote a revenue thesis, the company is missing plan, and nobody in the building can credibly explain the gap between the model and the actuals. The second is an **architecture problem**: the go-to-market motion that got the company to $8M or $15M in revenue physically cannot get it to $40M, and someone needs to redesign segmentation, coverage, comp, and the pipeline engine. The third is a **bridge problem**: the founder-seller-CEO is stepping back from revenue, or the incumbent VP of Sales just left, and there is a leadership vacuum the board cannot leave open for a six-month search.

A fractional CRO is exceptionally good at the first two and adequate at the third. What distinguishes the fractional operator from a management consultant is accountability to a number and authority over the team — they own quota attainment, not a deck. What distinguishes them from a full-time CRO is that you are renting judgment and pattern recognition, not building a permanent seat. For a PE-backed company where the deal thesis rests on commercial improvement, that pattern recognition is the entire point: a good fractional CRO has personally lived through four or five holds and knows which levers move EBITDA inside a two-to-five-year window and which are vanity projects. If your problem is genuinely "we don't know why the revenue engine is underperforming and we need someone who has fixed this exact thing before," fractional is close to ideal. If your problem is "we have a clear plan and just need someone to execute it with a team for the next four years," you are describing a full-time hire and should not talk yourself into fractional to save money. See the deeper breakdown of go-to-market diagnosis at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/rev-diagnosis-first-90.

## How do you decide between fractional, interim, and full-time for a PE hold?

The decision hinges on three variables: the **stage of the hold**, the **nature of the revenue gap**, and the **state of the existing team**. Early in a hold, when the diagnosis is unsettled and the model is still being pressure-tested, a fractional or interim leader gives the sponsor optionality — you buy senior judgment without locking in a hire before you understand the org. Later in a hold, when the motion is defined and the job is to recruit, coach, and retain a scaling team through an exit, the calculus flips hard toward full-time, because the CRO's value is now relational and durable rather than diagnostic.

The distinction between "fractional" and "interim" matters more than most boards realize. **Interim** means full-time hours for a fixed window — usually to stabilize a crisis or bridge a search — and typically commands near-full-time economics. **Fractional** means part-time on an ongoing basis, often across a small portfolio of engagements, at two to three days a week. A PE-backed company in genuine free-fall (a departed sales leader, a collapsing quarter, an angry board) usually needs interim intensity first, then can taper to fractional oversight once the fire is out. A company that is merely underperforming its model needs fractional from the start. Getting this wrong — hiring fractional bandwidth for a full-time crisis — is one of the most common early-hold mistakes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Revenue gap identified in PE hold] --> B{Is the motion already defined and working}
    B -->|Yes need durable team builder| C[Hire full time CRO]
    B -->|No needs diagnosis and redesign| D{How urgent is the crisis}
    D -->|Acute crisis full time hours| E[Interim CRO first then taper]
    D -->|Structural underperformance| F[Fractional CRO two to three days]
    F --> G[Diagnose fix and install operating system]
    E --> G
    G --> H{Is a permanent leader now needed}
    H -->|Yes scale phase| C
    H -->|No steady state oversight| F
```

The framework above is deliberately conservative: it pushes you toward full-time whenever the job is fundamentally about building and holding a team over years, and toward fractional whenever the job is fundamentally about diagnosis, architecture, and installing an operating system. Most first-year PE holds sit on the fractional-to-interim side of that line, which is exactly why the model has exploded in adoption. More on staging the first year at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/pe-first-year-revenue-playbook.

## What do the economics actually look like versus a full-time CRO?

This is where the case for fractional is strongest and also most frequently oversold. A full-time CRO at a lower-middle-market PE portfolio company typically costs a base in the mid-six figures, plus a variable component tied to the number, plus equity, plus the fully loaded burden of benefits, recruiting fees, and ramp time. Critically, a full-time executive search runs three to six months, and the new hire needs another one to two quarters to become productive — so the true cost of a full-time hire includes a half-year of continued underperformance while the seat is empty and another quarter of ramp. In a five-year hold, burning the first year on search-and-ramp is not a rounding error; it is a meaningful chunk of the value-creation window.

A fractional CRO inverts that curve. You are typically paying a monthly retainer for two to three days a week, with no recruiting fee, no ramp — a seasoned fractional operator is productive in week two — and no severance exposure if the fit is wrong. The retainer is materially below a loaded full-time package, and because the engagement is contractual, you can scale hours up during a crunch and down during steady-state without renegotiating an employment relationship. **The catch:** fractional economics only pencil out if the engagement produces durable structural change — a rebuilt comp plan, a functioning pipeline council, a hired-and-onboarded VP of Sales — rather than becoming an indefinite monthly line item that quietly becomes more expensive than the full-time hire you avoided. The failure mode is the "forever fractional" engagement that runs 30 months at retainer and leaves nothing behind. Structure the deal with an explicit deliverable set and an exit trigger, and the economics are compelling. Structure it as open-ended advisory, and you have simply hired an expensive contractor.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Sponsor needs revenue leadership] --> B[Full time path]
    A --> C[Fractional path]
    B --> B1[Search three to six months]
    B1 --> B2[Ramp one to two quarters]
    B2 --> B3[Full loaded package plus equity]
    C --> C1[Productive in week two]
    C1 --> C2[Monthly retainer no search fee]
    C2 --> C3[Scale hours up or down]
    B3 --> D{Time to first impact}
    C3 --> D
    D -->|Fractional is faster and cheaper early| E[Choose fractional for first phase]
    D -->|Full time wins for multi year scale| F[Choose full time for scale phase]
```

For a structured view of how to model the total cost of a revenue leadership decision — including the hidden cost of an empty seat — see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-cost-of-delay.

## What are the specific risks and failure modes in a PE context?

The PE context introduces risks that do not exist in a normal fractional engagement, and a board that ignores them tends to get burned. The **first risk is authority.** A fractional CRO who lacks explicit, board-communicated authority over the revenue org will be quietly ignored by a founder-CEO who resents the sponsor's involvement or by a sales team that treats a part-time leader as optional. The engagement only works if the board and CEO publicly delegate real decision rights — comp changes, hiring, firing, forecast ownership — to the fractional leader on day one. Ambiguity here is the single most common cause of failed engagements.

The **second risk is the residue problem.** Because the fractional CRO is temporary by design, there is a strong tendency to run the revenue org through their personal judgment rather than installing a durable operating system that survives their departure. A good engagement leaves behind documented processes, a functioning forecast cadence, a hired successor or a promotable internal leader, and a comp plan the next leader can run. A bad engagement leaves a spreadsheet only the fractional CRO understands and a team that regresses the moment they roll off. The **third risk is portfolio conflict** — a fractional operator serving several clients may not have the bandwidth your quarter demands, and their incentives are not perfectly aligned with your single hold. Vet capacity honestly and put a minimum-days commitment in writing. The **fourth risk is the exit narrative**: if you are within 18 months of a sale, the buyer's diligence team will ask who runs revenue, and "a part-time contractor" is a harder story to tell than "a full-time CRO with equity." Sequence the fractional-to-permanent transition so the org chart is clean before you go to market.

## How should a sponsor structure the engagement so it actually works?

Structure is where good intentions become results. Start with a **written 90-day diagnostic mandate** — the first engagement phase should be a bounded diagnosis with specific deliverables: a validated revenue model, a pipeline and coverage analysis, a segmentation and comp review, and a prioritized fix list mapped to the deal thesis. Do not let the engagement start as open-ended "help with sales." A crisp diagnostic phase forces the fractional CRO to prove pattern recognition fast and gives the board an early, cheap off-ramp if the fit is wrong.

Second, **tie compensation partially to outcomes.** The best PE-backed fractional engagements pair a base retainer with a success component tied to specific, measurable milestones — pipeline coverage ratio, forecast accuracy, net revenue retention, or a defined bookings target — so the operator's upside aligns with the deal thesis rather than with billing more hours. Third, **name the exit condition at the start.** Define what "done" looks like: a hired full-time CRO, an installed operating system, three consecutive quarters of forecast accuracy within a tolerance band. An engagement without a defined finish line drifts into forever-fractional. Fourth, **give them a board seat at the table** — the fractional CRO should present the revenue section of the board deck directly, because the sponsor's whole reason for the engagement is to get an unfiltered, operator-grade read on the number. Fifth and finally, **plan the succession from day one**: the fractional leader's job includes either developing an internal successor or running the search for their own replacement, so the transition to permanent leadership is a designed event and not a cliff.

## When is a fractional CRO clearly the wrong answer?

There are situations where the fractional model is a mistake dressed up as prudence, and recognizing them saves a wasted year. If the company's revenue problem is fundamentally about **team capacity** — you have a working motion and simply need more quota-carrying reps and a leader to recruit and hold them through a four-year scale — you need a full-time CRO with equity and a long runway, not a part-time diagnostician. Fractional leaders are architects and fixers; they are not, by design, the person who recruits and retains a 40-person sales org across a multi-year hold.

Likewise, if the sponsor's thesis rests on a **major go-to-market transformation** — a shift from founder-led sales to enterprise, a new product line requiring a net-new motion, a channel build — the depth and continuity of that work usually exceeds what two to three days a week can carry, and the company deserves a full-time leader who lives inside the transformation daily. And if the existing team has **deep trust and culture issues** that require a leader physically present to rebuild credibility, a part-time outsider will struggle to earn the standing needed to heal it. The rule of thumb: fractional wins when the scarce resource is *judgment and diagnosis*; full-time wins when the scarce resource is *presence, relationships, and durable team-building*. Name which one your hold actually needs before you sign anything.

## Related questions
### How much does a fractional CRO cost for a PE portfolio company?
Pricing is engagement-specific and varies by scope and hours, but it is structured as a monthly retainer for two to three days a week, materially below a loaded full-time package, often paired with an outcome-based success component tied to the deal thesis. Never quote a fixed figure without scoping hours and deliverables.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most PE-backed engagements run 6 to 18 months: a bounded 90-day diagnostic phase, a 6-to-12-month fix-and-install phase, and a planned transition to either a full-time successor or steady-state oversight. Open-ended engagements without an exit condition are a warning sign.

### Can a fractional CRO recruit and build the permanent sales team?
Partially. A strong fractional CRO can hire early key roles and run the search for their own full-time successor, but building and retaining a large quota-carrying org over years is durable relational work better suited to a permanent leader. Use fractional to design the team, full-time to hold it.

### What is the difference between an interim CRO and a fractional CRO?
Interim means full-time hours for a fixed crisis or bridge window at near-full-time economics; fractional means part-time (two to three days a week) on an ongoing basis, often across a small portfolio. Acute crises need interim intensity first; structural underperformance suits fractional from the start.

### Does a fractional CRO get equity in a PE-backed company?
Sometimes, but the more common structure is a base retainer plus an outcome-based success fee tied to measurable milestones rather than a full equity grant. Meaningful equity is more typical for the eventual full-time CRO who will carry the org through to exit.

## FAQ
**Will a fractional CRO have enough authority to change comp and fire underperformers?**
Only if the board and CEO explicitly delegate that authority on day one and communicate it to the team. Authority ambiguity is the single most common cause of failed engagements — put decision rights in writing before the engagement starts.

**How fast should we expect results from a fractional CRO?**
A seasoned fractional operator is productive within about two weeks and should deliver a validated diagnosis and prioritized fix list within 90 days. Durable structural improvements — comp redesign, forecast accuracy, pipeline coverage — typically show over one to three quarters.

**What happens to the revenue org when the fractional CRO rolls off?**
That depends entirely on whether they installed a durable operating system or ran the org through personal judgment. Insist the engagement produce documented processes, a forecast cadence, and a named successor so the team does not regress on departure.

**Is a fractional CRO a red flag to a future buyer in diligence?**
It can be if it is unresolved at sale. A part-time contractor running revenue is a weaker diligence story than a full-time leader with equity, so sequence the transition to permanent leadership so the org chart is clean before you go to market.

**Can one fractional CRO serve multiple PE portfolio companies at once?**
Yes, and most do — that is the model. The risk is capacity: confirm a minimum-days commitment in writing and vet that your quarter's demands fit within their available bandwidth before signing.

**Should the fractional CRO present to the board directly?**
Yes. The sponsor's core reason for the engagement is an unfiltered, operator-grade read on the number, so the fractional CRO should own and present the revenue section of the board deck rather than filtering it through the CEO.

**How do we know if we need fractional versus full-time?**
Ask what the scarce resource is. If it is judgment, diagnosis, and go-to-market architecture, choose fractional. If it is presence, relationships, and building and holding a large team across a multi-year scale-up, choose full-time.
